newsitem.title: INDIA: India closer to finding $5 bln oil stain remover.
newsitem.headline: India closer to finding $5 bln oil stain remover.

text.p: A 5.3 billion dollar oil stain over India's national accounts may be absorbed into the government's fiscal deficit.
The Press Trust of India on Monday reported the Finance Ministry had done its sums, and reckoned it could afford to carry the burden on its books.
That would wipe out a multi-billion dollar debt to domestic oil companies for selling petroleum products below market prices to support the government's subsidy regime.

Finance Ministry sources said consolidating the 190 billion rupee ($5.3 billion) debt, which currently lies on the oil pool account managed seperately by India's Oil Coordination Committee, would not push the fiscal deficit above 5.3 percent of gross domestic product.
That means kissing goodbye the 1997/98 (April-March) budget target for a deficit of 4.5 percent of GDP, but the ministry sources said the extra burden was manageable, PTI said.

The oil pool deficit is the stickiest and most pressing economic problem facing Prime Minister Inder Gujral's government. The mess is a result of India leaving its domestic prices unchanged when world oil prices surged late last year. Dr R.K. Pachouri, head of the independent Tata Energy Research Insititute, believed the government was close to a concensus on taking over the debt and also on agreeing a small price rise for some products.
"I think the way the way things are heading they will pass on the debt to the government's own fiscal deficit," he said.
A committee charged with seeking ways to restructure the oil sector's finances suggested the oil debt could be paid for by issuing "petro-bonds".
Sources in New Delhi said the government could announce measures in August, but the timing remained unclear as Gujral's fragile coalition lurched into more trouble on Monday.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, a southern regional party, announced it was planning to leave the government but support it from outside, in protest against the behaviour of some unidentified coalition partners.

The latest squabble does not bode will for convening the coalition's policy-making steering committee. The committee has failed in its last two meetings to solve the oil riddle, and a third meeting has been deferred several times already.

But the oil companies need money back fast to pay for crude oil supplies needed to keep their refineries working. They are already heavily indebted and are keeping supplies flowing on a hand-to-mouth basis.
Politicians are on alert to the possibility of mid-term polls as the centre-left coalition commands only the third largest bloc in parliament.
It is also riven with internal squabbles and dependent on support from the opposition Congress party which brought down Gujral's predecessor H.D. Deve Gowda in April.
While Gujral's government might be safe for now, the ever-present fear of mid-term elections has stopped it from taking unpopular steps, like raising oil prices.

"The government is pussy footing on this. No political party will publicly support the dismantling of the administered pricing mechanism," V.Raghuraman, secretary general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said on Monday.
